cells.tense: You're the one deciding what's finished in this clearing, and the deciding sits steady in you.
cells.ask: Say one ending out loud as finished, not paused, where someone close to it can hear you — so the space it leaves belongs to you instead of staying a topic in the room.
cells.core:
Two needs can sit in your hands at once — what's ending and what's arriving both get tended, neither gets dropped, and the work doesn't cost you more than you meant to spend. What's closing gets the same attention as what's opening, you're not bracing through it, and people near you can feel that nothing here is being pushed. The clearing moves at its own speed and you move with it, steady and unhurried, and when something is done you can set it down without needing the next thing already planted.

Finish one thing where it can be heard. Notice whether the closing feels lighter once someone else knows it happened instead of staying your private fact.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one deciding what's finished here, not just what's next.

cells.place: the clearing where something has to fully end before what's next can start

cells.tense: You're living past this ending already, putting your hand on the next thing before this one has cleared the ground.
cells.ask: Pick one ending you've been trying to rush and let it finish at its own pace this week — no pushing the next thing into the open space until the old one is actually gone.
cells.core:
Care at the right speed lets effort go where it's asked for, keeps the hands open, and lets growth happen on its own schedule without anyone dragging it. Run ahead of itself, that same care grips: you're tending a next thing that hasn't arrived, both hands on it, calling the grip responsibility, and the tightness reads as duty from the inside. The grip keeps the ground unclear, and the ground is what you need.

An ending that finishes on its own gives you something a rushed one can't. Let one thing close without you managing the exit, and see what the cleared space will actually hold.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing the next garden before this one's been cleared.
cells.verb: tending what's growing through form — holding competing demands together with care rather than force
cells.place: the clearing where something has to fully end before what's next can start

cells.tense: You're back at a door that closed already, tending something finished or looking past the clearing in front of you.
cells.ask: Walk through one room where you live and move one thing that belongs to what's ended — out of sight, out of the way, gone — and let the floor show what's actually here now.
cells.core:
Tending that holds without clutching lets growth happen at its own pace, and when this is clean you can feel the difference between keeping something and keeping watch over it. What's here instead is watch kept over something already done — and the watch has a kind of tending in it too, which is why it's hard to catch. A clearing done right leaves open ground for whatever's next, and yours is still crowded with what's finished.

Ending one thing doesn't require the next one to be figured out yet. Move the object, and the floor will tell you what it's willing to hold.
cells.sheetLine: The thing you're tending has already ended — you just haven't let it.

cells.tense: The endings are moving through your own hands, and you talk about them like something that happened to you.
cells.ask: Write down one ending you've been calling inevitable, or necessary, or just how things go — and read the sentence back with your own name as the one who decided it.
cells.core:
You've been doing the hard part: letting things finish, keeping the space while they do, not forcing what wants to close, and that's the work running clean and already yours. The story you tell yourself says it arrived, or that you're managing it, so the one doing the work gets no credit in their own account — and after a while that reads as drift, endings you'd rather have kept, work that cost you and never got counted.

A clearing you haven't owned can't feed the next thing the way a chosen one can. Look at one ending you've been calling a fact of life, and try saying it was a decision you made.
cells.sheetLine: The endings are yours. You've been talking about them like they aren't.
